newsitem.title: CAMBODIA: Cambodian king will not amnesty exiled prince.
newsitem.headline: Cambodian king will not amnesty exiled prince.

text.p: King Norodom Sihanouk said on Wednesday he would not grant amnesty to exiled Prince Norodom Sirividh, paving the way for the imprisonment of the king's half-brother if he returns to Cambodia.
"As for Prince Norodom Sirivudh, my half-brother, I apologise to his close relations and his supporters: I cannot amnesty him," the king wrote in an interview with his cabinet released on Wednesday.
The statement comes after nearly two weeks of controversy over the planned return of Sirivudh, who was sentenced for an alleged plot to assassinate co-Premier Hun Sen.
Sirivudh was exiled to France nearly one year ago to avoid imprisonment, but was sentenced to 10 years' jail in his absence. International observers branded the trial a travesty.
Sirivudh has said he will return even if he faces imprisonment because he can no longer afford to live in France.
The prince's vow to return to Cambodia angered Hun Sen, won support from Cambodia's other co-premier, Prince Norodom Ranariddh, and inspired caution on the part of the king, who brokered his exile.
Legal analysts said Sihanouk declined to pardon Sirivudh over fear of Hun Sen's reaction and possible political or military repercussions.
"I think Sihanouk knew if he didn't have the express permission of Hun Sen...the amnesty could create major political problems," said one analyst.
"The king knows he has the constitutional right to grant amnesty, but that decision could destabilise the country politically and militarily."
Hun Sen threatened to call out troops and tanks to prevent Sirivudh's return, but later said he would welcome Sirivudh with flowers -- if he were granted amnesty by the king.
Sihanouk in turn said he would not grant amnesty to Sirivudh without the approval of both prime ministers.
While Ranariddh wrote a letter supporting the royal pardon, Hun Sen told Reuters it was not his place to request the amnesty, and that he would not ask for the pardon "until I die".
Political analysts said Sihanouk's decision not to grant amnesty to Sirivudh showed a desire to sidestep the controversy for now.

In his statement, Sihanouk gave no direct explanation for his decision, but he did take issue with Hun Sen's recent comment in an interview with Reuters that the king did not need to seek permission from the co-premiers before granting amnesty.

Sihanouk noted that he had solicited the co-premiers' opinions in special cases, and recalled bowing to Hun Sen's opposition when deciding not to grant full amnesty to Prince Norodom Chakrapong and Generals Sin Sen and Sin Song for a 1993 coup attempt.

Analysts said the tangle over Sirivudh's fate showed the precarious position the king was in, and the deep divisions between the co-premiers since they formed their uneasy coalition following U.N.-sponsored elections in 1993.
They said Sirivudh's planned return would be a further test of the two leaders' relations, since Hun Sen has said that if the exiled prince is not amnestied, he must be jailed.

"I think the king will have to come back to this issue in the near future," said one political analyst. "He wants the controversy to die down now, but later on...if Sirivudh is jailed...he may take a more decisive approach."
